newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten in HK church praises wealth on last Sunday.
newsitem.headline: Patten in HK church praises wealth on last Sunday.

text.p: Governor Chris Patten went to church as usual on his last Sunday in Hong Kong and took to the pulpit to tell the congregation it was no crime to be rich.
Accompanied by his wife, Lavender, and three daughters, Patten attended Mass at his local parish church -- the Roman Catholic Cathedral of Hong Kong a short stroll from the governor's mansion.
Patten's job will come to an end at midnight on Monday, June 30, when 156 years of British colonial rule end and fiercely capitalistic Hong Kong reverts to China.

His final days in office have been hectic for the 28th and last Governor, and Patten, a staunch Catholic who had a large crucifix positioned over his desk in Government House during his five-year tenure, apologised to the congregation for having to slip away promptly after the service.
He had to get back to Government House, he said, in time to greet British royal heir Prince Charles who would hand out the last British knighthoods and awards to Hong Kong people.
Catholic Priest John Tsang marked the occasion by presenting a framed icon of the Madonna and Child to his most famous parishioner.
Patten then told the congregation he would miss the vibrancy of a Hong Kong he had earlier described as "a great Chinese success story with British characteristics".
Being rich was no crime, the former British Conservative Party career-politician said, quoting the Biblical parable of the talents about three brothers given a stipend and sent out to the world.
The brother who invested his wisely so that it appreciated in value is praised in the Bible.
Hong Kong's per capita gross domestic product of around US$26,000 outstrips that in Britain.
"The main reason why I am confident about Hong Kong's future is because of Hong Kong itself," Patten said.
"We very often talk about it being a rich and prosperous society and actually we are. We're rather good at making money."
Patten said he would miss the parish that had been part of his life for five years.
"I've no doubt at all that I've enjoyed practising my religion here in Hong Kong more than ever before."
Officially-atheist China has promised to respect freedom of religion in Hong Kong, along with the other liberties cherished in the territory, for 50 years after the handover.
But some leaders of various faiths have expressed unease about their future.
Last month, Hong Kong's Bishop Joseph Zen and two senior clerics visited China to discuss the Catholic Church's future under the rule of communist Chinese leaders.
They said their frank and friendly talks had "strengthened our confidence". Pope John Paul sent his blessings to Hong Kong and Chinese Roman Catholics on Friday, wishing them well after the handover.
